```{=html}
<div class="shots">
  <figure><img src="figs/screens/model-builder-tile.png" alt="Model Builder: the diagram of a three-loop PWR, with its pumps, steam generators and injection systems">
    <figcaption><b>Model Builder</b>choose the domain, configure components and initial conditions, schedule operator actions</figcaption></figure>
  <figure><img src="figs/screens/monitor-tile.png" alt="Monitor: a Gantt chart of sequences forking at branch points">

  <figure><img src="figs/screens/results-tile.png" alt="Results: a graph of pivotal events over simulation time">
```

::: {style="font-size:0.78em; margin-top:0.5em;"}
Checkpoint and restore branching, pivotal events from trip firings, lumping
of simultaneous trips: **no MPI, no Fortran, no local toolchain.**
:::

::: {style="font-size:0.66em; color:#555555; margin-top:0.5em;"}
Branching here comes from scheduled operator actions and trip firings; the
cognitive branching of the IDAC crew model stays in the C++ engine, which
drives the same solvers through the same contract. A solver that runs here is
ready for the parallel engine.
:::

::: {.notes}
The same interface also makes the method easier to get into. A web workflow
builds dynamic event trees from a browser, against any solver that implements
the interface.

In the model builder, on the left, you choose the domain, configure the plant,
and schedule operator actions. The monitor, in the middle, shows the tree
growing live: every bar is a sequence, forking at branch points. And the
results view, on the right, is an interactive plot of the pivotal events. None
of it needs MPI, Fortran, or a local toolchain.

One clarification. Branching here comes from scheduled operator actions and
trip firings; the cognitive branching of the IDAC crew model stays in the C++
engine, which drives the same solvers through the same interface.
:::

## One interface, two very different reactors {#two-reactors data-section="4"}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
| | **PWR** | **Space reactor** |
|:------|:-----------------------|:-----------------------|
| **plant** | generic three-loop benchmark | nuclear electric propulsion |
| **solver** | RELAP5/MOD3.3, and a lumped service in a few hundred lines | a solver service with its mapper |
| **signals** | 15 control variables (lumped service) | 32 control variables, 40 trips |
| **actions** | operator actions in a loss of offsite power | drum adjustment, load shedding, converter restart |
| **responder** | a control-room crew | a software policy, in the crew's slot |
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
```{=html}
<figure class="schem fade">
  <img src="figs/screens/space-reactor-core.png" alt="Schematic of the space reactor in the Model Builder: a reactor with six control drums and a shield, twelve sodium heat pipes, a closed Brayton converter and four radiator panels">
  <figcaption>The space fission reactor in the same Model Builder: a model built from public SR-1 Freedom information.</figcaption>
</figure>
```
:::
::::

::: {style="font-size:0.86em; margin-top:0.45em;"}
The contract, the branching logic, the browser workflow and the analysis
tooling are the same for both;
[only the solver service and its mapper differ.]{style="color:#B40000;"}
:::

::: {.slideref}
A third solver, a race-car dynamics model, exists only to show that nothing in the contract is nuclear-specific.
:::

::: {.notes}
Does the interface really work for any solver? The paper tests that with two
very different plants behind the same interface.

The first is the PWR: RELAP5 at full fidelity, and beside it a lumped PWR
service that implements the interface in a few hundred lines.

The second, in the picture, is a compact space fission reactor for nuclear
electric propulsion: control drums, heat pipes, a closed Brayton converter,
radiators, and Hall thrusters, with thirty-two control variables and forty
trips. It is built from the public information on NASA's SR-1 Freedom.

The space reactor was chosen on purpose. With remote and autonomous operation,
a software policy takes the place of the control-room crew, and this is an
area where dynamic PRA has no established tooling. Between the two reactors,
only the solver service and its mapper differ.
:::
